chapters.title: Chapter 2 — Human Resources
intro: In the end, information security depends on people. The best firewall cannot stop an employee who sends drawings to a private mailbox. The strictest access control cannot stop a colleague who is tricked into opening the door by social engineering. ISA Chapter 2 "Human Resources" follows the employee lifecycle: qualification checks before someone joins (2.1.1), non-disclosure and compliance obligations when the contract is signed (2.1.2), training and awareness during employment (2.1.3), and rules for mobile work outside the security zones (2.1.4).

Most of the four controls in this chapter are led by HR, but information security, IT, legal and line managers must also take part. For automotive suppliers, the most common gaps are: temporary agency workers and outsourced staff are not covered, training is only given to new hires, and there are no written rules for working from home. After this chapter you should be able to identify the security steps that are missing from your own people-management processes.

blocks.title: Who is "all staff"?
blocks.text: In principle, the ISA people-related requirements cover permanent employees, fixed-term staff, temporary agency workers, interns, and external people who work on site long-term and can access company information. For external people, you can require their employer by contract to apply equivalent controls, and link this to supplier management in Chapter 6.
Note this down! Most Chapter 2 evidence sits with HR: job descriptions, signed confidentiality agreements, training records. Remember to prepare together with HR before the assessment!

controls.title: Qualification of employees for sensitive work fields
controls.q_en: To what extent is the qualification of employees for sensitive work fields ensured?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is the qualification of employees for sensitive work fields ensured?
controls.objective: Competent, reliable and trustworthy employees are essential for information security within the organization. Therefore, it is important to check the qualifications of potential employees (e.g., applicants) to an appropriate extent.

must: Sensitive work fields and jobs are determined.
The requirements for employees with respect to their job profiles are determined and fulfilled.
The identity of potential employees is verified (e.g., checking identity documents).
should: The personal suitability of potential employees is verified by means of simple methods (e.g., job interview).

An extended suitability verification depending on the respective work field and job is conducted (e.g., assessment centre, psychological analysis, checking of references, certificates and diploma, checking of certificates of conduct, checking of professional and private background).

controls.refs: ISO 27001:2022 A.6.1 | ISA/IEC 62443-2-1 6.2.2 | NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-04, PR.AT-02 | BSI IT-Grundschutz ORP.2 | NIST SP800-53r5 PS-2, PS-3, PS-7, PS-9, SA-21
explain: 2.1.1 is about security "before a person comes through the door". The three must requirements form a chain: first find out which work fields and jobs are **sensitive** (for example IT system administrators, R&D and design, HR and payroll, finance, staff working with prototypes or test vehicles, people with access to customer networks). Then define the required skills, certificates and trustworthiness for these jobs in the job descriptions. Finally, when hiring, at least **verify the identity**, so you know the applicant is really the person on the ID document.

The should requirements have two levels. General suitability is checked with simple methods (a job interview). For sensitive jobs, extended checks are done based on risk, for example references from former employers, checking that diplomas and certificates are genuine, professional certifications, or even a certificate of good conduct. The original text lists many methods, but it does not require all of them. You choose the right depth "depending on the work field and job". What matters is that you have a basis for the decision and apply it consistently.

In practice, background checks must also comply with data-protection and employment law (for example the EU GDPR, or Taiwan's PDPA and Employment Service Act). For example, you may not ask applicants for private data that has nothing to do with the job, and collecting a police certificate or contacting a former employer needs the person's consent and must be limited to what the job requires. We recommend that HR and legal create a "background check list for sensitive jobs" together, stating clearly what is checked, which consents are needed and how long the data is kept.

This control also applies to agency workers and external people who work on site long-term. The ISA must requirement says "potential employees", and auditors often ask: are outsourced IT engineers and agency operators checked by their agency? Is this agreed in the contract? You can explain this together with supplier management in 6.1.1.
practice: Create a "sensitive jobs list": job title, department, reason for sensitivity (e.g., system administration rights, access to prototypes, access to customer confidential information) and required check level. Review it once a year as the organization changes.
Add an "information security requirements" section to each job description, for example required certificates, documents to sign, and onboarding security training to complete.
At onboarding, HR checks the original ID document and keeps a record of the check (only "checked, by whom, date" — no need to copy the whole ID, in line with data minimization).

Before hiring for a sensitive job, run extended checks: verify diplomas and certificates, contact former employers (with written consent), ask for a police certificate where necessary, and keep the results on a "background check record form".

Agency and outsourced staff: require the agency or contractor in the contract to perform equivalent checks and provide a declaration. The requesting department confirms this before the person starts on site.
When an employee moves internally into a sensitive job (for example an operator becomes an MES system administrator), check qualifications and check level again, as for a new hire.

questions: How does your organization define sensitive work fields and jobs? Where is the list?
Please explain the qualification requirements for the system administrator role, and how the most recently hired administrator was verified against them.
How is the identity of new hires verified at onboarding? Who is responsible? Is there a record?
Which extended checks are done for sensitive jobs? How do you get the person's consent?
How are the qualifications of agency workers or on-site outsourced engineers confirmed?
Is a new assessment done when an employee moves internally into a sensitive job?
evidence: Sensitive jobs list and the criteria used
Job descriptions that include security requirements
New-hire onboarding checklist (with an identity check field)
Background check consent forms and check records (sample)
Personnel screening clauses in agency or outsourcing contracts
findings: Job descriptions exist, but no jobs are identified as sensitive. All jobs are treated the same, and there is no basis for the depth of checks.
No record is kept of identity checks for new hires, so there is no proof they were done.
The system administrator job requires a specific certificate, but the sampled person does not have it, and there is no plan to close the gap.
Agency workers start working directly; the contract does not require the agency to perform identity or background checks.

controls.tip: Allan's tip: More background checks are not always better. Check sensitive jobs in depth and other jobs just enough — and always get consent. Otherwise you fix security but create a data-protection problem.

controls.title: Contractual obligation of staff to comply with IS policies
controls.q_en: To what extent is all staff contractually bound to comply with information security policies?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is all staff contractually bound to comply with information security policies?
controls.objective: Organizations are subject to legislation, regulations and internal policies. Already when hiring staff, it must be ensured that employees commit to compliance with the policies and are aware of the consequences of misconduct.

must: A non-disclosure obligation is in effect.
An obligation to comply with the information security policies is in effect.
should: A non-disclosure obligation beyond the employment contract is in effect.
Information security aspects are considered in the employment contracts of the staff.
A procedure for handling violations of said obligations is described.

controls.refs: ISO 27001:2022 A.6.2, A.6.5 | BSI IT-Grundschutz ORP.2 | NIST SP800-53r5 PL-4, PS-4, PS-6, PS-8
explain: The key words in the control question are **all staff**: not only permanent employees, but also agency workers, interns, student workers and external people working on site long-term. There are only two must requirements, but both must be "in effect": the non-disclosure obligation and the obligation to comply with the information security policies. "In effect" means signed, dated and traceable to the current staff list — not just a template.

The should requirements go further: the non-disclosure obligation continues after employment ends (for example, trade secrets and customer information remain confidential after the person leaves), security clauses are included in the employment contract or work rules, and there is a procedure for handling violations (for example disciplinary action under the work rules or civil claims), so employees clearly know the consequences.

Note: a common setup is a three-part package of "employment contract + confidentiality agreement + work rules". Work rules (in Taiwan, for example, registered with the labor authority) bind all employees and can include compliance with security policies and sanctions for violations. The confidentiality agreement can define a confidentiality period after leaving. Trade secret law (such as the EU Trade Secrets Directive or Taiwan's Trade Secrets Act) also provides a legal basis, but only if the company has taken "reasonable measures to keep the information secret" — and signed confidentiality documents are one piece of evidence for such measures.

This control is often linked with 2.1.3 (training), 6.1.2 (NDAs with external parties) and 1.1.1 (publishing the policy). If employees sign that they will "comply with the security policies", you must be able to show that the policies are published, accessible to employees and covered in training. Otherwise the contractual obligation will be seen as a formality only.
practice: Create an "employee confidentiality and security compliance agreement" covering the scope of confidentiality, the period after leaving, compliance with company security policies and procedures, and how violations are handled. It is signed on the first day.

Update the work rules and employment contract templates with security clauses (for example: do not take confidential data out without permission, do not use unapproved software, report security incidents).
Agency workers, interns and on-site contractor staff all sign a personal confidentiality agreement, or their employer signs and provides a list of the people concerned.
Define an "information security violation procedure": violation levels, investigation process, sanctions mapped to work-rule clauses, integrated with the HR disciplinary process.

Every year, compare signed records with the current staff list to confirm 100% coverage. At exit, the leaving form reminds the person of the confidentiality obligation and asks them to sign an exit confidentiality statement.
When the policy changes significantly, use electronic sign-off (for example M365 Forms or the HR system) so employees confirm again that they have read it and agree to comply.

questions: Please show the template for the employee non-disclosure obligation and the signed records of three sampled new hires.
How are agency workers, interns and on-site contractors bound by confidentiality?
Does the confidentiality obligation remain valid after an employee leaves? For how long?
How do employees commit to complying with the security policies? When a policy changes, how are they informed?
What is the procedure if an employee violates a security policy? Have there been any recent cases?
evidence: Employment contract template and work rules (with security clauses)
Confidentiality agreements and signed records (sampled against the staff list)
Exit confidentiality statements
Security violation procedure and disciplinary records (if any)
Confidentiality agreements or contract clauses for external people
findings: All permanent employees signed confidentiality agreements, but agency workers and interns have no confidentiality obligation at all.
The confidentiality clause only applies during employment; there is no obligation after leaving and no reminder at exit.
The contract says to follow company rules, but does not explicitly include the information security policies.
There is no violation procedure. An employee once sent drawings outside without permission and only received a verbal warning, with no record.

controls.tip: Allan's tip: Auditors love to pick random names from the staff list and check the signed records. Do this check yourself once a year — it is much better than being caught with missing documents.

controls.title: Security awareness and training of staff
controls.q_en: To what extent is staff made aware of and trained with respect to the risks arising from the handling of information?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is staff made aware of and trained with respect to the risks arising from the handling of information?
controls.objective: If the requirements and risks of information security are not known to the employees, there is a risk of misconduct resulting in damage to the organization. Therefore, it is important that information security is internalized and practiced as a natural part of their work.

must: Employees are trained and made aware.
should: A concept for awareness and training of employees is prepared. The following aspects are considered: – Information security policy; – Reporting of information security events; – Reaction to occurrence of malware; – Policies regarding user accounts and login information (e.g., password policy); – Compliance issues of information security; – Requirements and procedures regarding the use of non-disclosure agreements when sharing information requiring protection; – Use of external IT services.

Target groups for training and awareness measures (i.e., people working in specific risk environments such as managers including organizational leaders, administrators, employees having access to customer networks, personnel in areas of manufacturing) are identified and considered in a training concept.
The concept has been approved by the responsible management.
Training and awareness measures are carried out both at regular intervals and in response to events.
Participation in training and awareness measures is documented.
Contact persons for information security are known to employees.

controls.refs: ISO 27001:2022 7.2, 7.3, A.6.3 | ISA/IEC 62443-2-1 6.2.4 | NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AT-01, PR.AT-02, GV.RR-01, GV.RR-02, GV.OC-02, GV.RR-04 | BSI IT-Grundschutz ORP.2 | NIST SP800-53r5 AT-2(2), AT-2(3), AT-3, AT-3(5), AT-4, AT-6, IR-2, IR-3, AC-21(1), PM-12, PM-13, SA-16
controls.change2027: ISA 2027 adds a dedicated training requirement for senior management and executive leadership to the target groups. At the same time, the former 5.2.3 should requirement on "case-by-case staff awareness" was deleted; it is now covered by 2.1.3.
explain: The must requirement is only one sentence: "Employees are trained and made aware." It looks simple, but maturity level 3 expects a systematic training concept, and that means the six should items: a concept, target groups, management approval, regular and event-driven measures, records, and employees who know whom to contact.

The training concept must cover seven topics: the security policy, incident reporting, what to do in case of malware, account and password rules, compliance, signing an NDA before sharing confidential information, and rules for external IT services (for example cloud services and generative AI tools). Auditors often compare these seven topics one by one with the table of contents of your training material, so it is best if your outline maps to them directly.

ISA 2027 puts special focus on **target groups**: managers (including organizational leaders), system administrators, employees with access to customer networks, and staff in manufacturing areas. Senior managers are frequent targets of social engineering (for example CEO fraud or fake payment requests). Production staff may have no computer and rarely read e-mail, so the training format must be adapted, for example short talks in shift meetings, posters and short videos.

"In response to events" means targeted awareness after a security incident, a new threat (for example a large phishing wave) or a policy change. This is also where maturity levels differ: annual training only shows that something is "performed"; adjusting quickly to events shows that it is really "managed".
practice: Create an "annual security training plan": target groups, topics, format, frequency, owner and completion target, approved by the CISO or the managing director.
New hires complete basic security training (online course plus test) within one week of joining. Until they complete it, they do not get access to confidential folders.

All staff receive security awareness training at least once a year, plus quarterly phishing simulations (for example with M365 Defender Attack Simulation or a third-party platform). People who click receive follow-up training.

Target-group training: senior managers focus on social engineering and crisis decisions; system administrators focus on privileged accounts and change management; production staff get five-minute talks in shift meetings and rules for USB devices and OT equipment.
Event-driven awareness: after an incident or a new type of fraud, publish a security alert within 48 hours (Teams, an official chat channel such as WhatsApp or LINE, notice boards).
Keep training records and test results in an LMS or on attendance lists. Calculate the completion rate every year and include it in the management review.
Show the security contact and how to report on the intranet home page, notice boards and desktop wallpaper (phone extension, e-mail, form link).

questions: Please show this year's security training plan. Who approved it?
Does the training cover incident reporting, malware response, password policy, NDAs and the use of external IT services?
Is there different training for managers, system administrators and production staff?
After the most recent security incident or threat, was there targeted awareness communication?
Please show the attendance records. What happens to people who did not attend?
(Interviewing an employee on site) If you suspected your computer had malware, what would you do? Who is your security contact?
evidence: Approved annual security training plan
Training material and outline (mapped to the seven topics)
Attendance lists or LMS completion reports, test results
Phishing simulation reports and follow-up training records
Security alerts published after events
Screenshots or photos of posters showing the security contact
findings: Only new hires are trained; current employees have not received any security training for years.
The training plan is not approved by management and no target groups are identified; managers and production staff all take the same course.
Training records are incomplete, so the completion rate cannot be proven, and people who did not attend are not followed up.
Employees interviewed on site do not know whom to report a security incident to.
The training material does not cover rules for external IT services (such as free cloud storage or AI tools).

controls.tip: Allan's tip: Auditors randomly ask employees on site "Who do you call if you get malware?" Not knowing the answer hurts more than a missing attendance list. Put the contact details where everyone can see them.

controls.title: Regulation of mobile work
controls.q_en: To what extent is mobile work regulated?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is mobile work regulated?
controls.objective: Working outside the specifically defined security zones (mobile work) creates risks requiring corresponding protective measures.

must: The requirements for mobile work are determined and fulfilled. The following aspects are considered: – Behavior in private surroundings (e.g., working in a dedicated office at home or in a coworking space); – Behavior in public surroundings (e.g., during travels, shared office in a coworking space); – Secure handling of and access to information (in both electronic and paper form) while considering the protection needs and the contractual requirements applying to private and public surroundings; – Protection from theft in public surroundings; – Measures to ensure a secure access to organization’s IT-services.
should: The following aspects are considered: – Measures for travelling (e.g., viewing by authorities); – Measures for travelling to security-critical countries.
Employee awareness.
high: Protective measures against overhearing and viewing are implemented. (C)

controls.refs: ISO 27001:2022 A.6.7, A.8.1 | ISA/IEC 62443-2-1 8.4.2 | BSI IT-Grundschutz INF.8, INF.9, CON.7, NET.3.3 | NIST SP800-53r5 PE-17
controls.change2027: ISA 2027 rewrote the wording of the must requirement. It now clearly separates private surroundings (including home office and coworking space) from public surroundings, and adds measures for secure access to the organization's IT services. ISA 2027.1 also adds "coworking space" and "office-less" to the definitions.
explain: Mobile work means handling company information outside the security zones defined by the company: working from home, in a coworking space, on a train during a business trip, at an airport or in a customer's meeting room. The 2.1.4 must requirement lists the five aspects to consider very clearly: behavior in private surroundings, behavior in public surroundings, secure handling of information (including paper), theft protection, and secure access to company IT services.

Note the ISA 2027.1 definition of a coworking space: a shared office environment provided by a third party that is not part of the organization's ISMS. In other words, a coworking space is not a company security zone. The original text places it in both private surroundings (a dedicated office) and public surroundings (shared open seating), which means you must decide the protection level based on the actual situation.

"Considering the protection needs and the contractual requirements" is important. Many OEM project contracts require that confidential data is processed only on company premises, or forbid opening it in public places. Your mobile work rules must reflect such contractual limits, for example: drawings classified as "strictly confidential" may not be opened or printed at home or in public.

The should requirements mention possible viewing by authorities during travel (for example being asked to unlock a laptop at the border) and measures for travel to security-critical countries. A common solution is a clean travel laptop (loaner laptop). High protection needs (C) require protection against overhearing and viewing, for example privacy screen filters, no confidential calls in public places, and headsets for video meetings.
practice: Create a "mobile work policy": scope (home, coworking, travel, customer site), approval process, which data classes may be handled, and what is forbidden.

Technical measures: full-disk encryption on laptops (BitLocker or FileVault), access to internal systems via VPN or ZTNA with MFA, compliance management with Intune or another MDM, and non-compliant devices blocked (conditional access).

Paper documents: confidential paper documents are generally not taken home. If necessary, they are registered and kept in a lockable container. Documents to be destroyed are brought back to the office for shredding, never thrown into household waste.
Theft protection: never leave a laptop unattended in public places or visible in a car. Loss must be reported within the defined time (linked to 1.6.1).
High protection needs: provide privacy screen filters and headsets, do not hold confidential meetings in open spaces, and use background blur or a virtual background.

Travel rules: for high-risk countries, use dedicated travel laptops and phones, carry only the data you need, and reinstall or check the devices after returning. Explain how to act and report if customs inspects a device.
Raise awareness with annual training and a mobile work self-check list (for example: has the default password of the home router been changed, is there a separate workspace).

questions: Does the company allow working from home or in coworking spaces? Where are the rules?
How do employees access company systems from home or while travelling? Is MFA used?
Do customer contracts restrict where data may be processed? How do the mobile work rules reflect this?
May confidential paper documents be taken out of the company? How is this controlled?
If an employee loses a laptop on a train or at an airport, what must they do?
Are there special measures for business trips to high-risk countries?
(High protection needs) How do you prevent overhearing and viewing in public places?
evidence: Mobile work policy or home office rules
VPN or ZTNA and MFA configuration screenshots, conditional access policies
Device encryption status report (Intune or MDM)
Loan records for dedicated travel devices
Records of privacy filter distribution, mobile work training records
findings: The company actually allows working from home, but there are no written rules, only verbal approval by managers.
The rules only cover electronic data, not taking paper documents out or destroying them.
VPN login uses only username and password, with no additional authentication.
The customer contract forbids processing drawings outside the company, but the mobile work rules do not reflect this, and R&D staff open them at home as usual.

controls.tip: Allan's tip: Since the pandemic, many companies work from home "by habit" but never wrote it down as a rule. A TISAX auditor who sees VPN connection logs will ask about it, so first document the current situation, then improve it.

summary: 2.1.1: First identify sensitive jobs, then set qualification requirements in the job descriptions. Verify the identity of every potential employee; for sensitive jobs, add risk-based extended checks, and respect the consent rules of data-protection law.

2.1.2: The non-disclosure obligation and the obligation to comply with security policies must be "in effect" and cover all staff, including agency workers and external people. Ideally they continue after the person leaves, and there is a procedure for handling violations.

2.1.3: Training must be planned, approved by management, cover the seven main topics, target specific groups (including senior management and production staff), run regularly and in response to events, be recorded, and employees must know their security contact.

2.1.4: Mobile work must consider private and public surroundings, paper and electronic information, theft protection and secure remote access. For high protection needs, protect against overhearing and viewing.
Key ISA 2027 changes: 2.1.3 adds dedicated training for senior management, and the 2.1.4 must requirement was rewritten and introduces the coworking space concept.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — Physical Security
intro: Chapter 3 is about the security you can "see and touch": security zones, supporting assets, and mobile devices that leave the company. Physical security is especially important in the automotive supply chain, because drawings, samples and test data often exist at the same time on paper, on hard drives, on laptops and as physical parts. If any one of these carriers gets out of control, the information leaks.

This chapter covers 3.1.1 security zone management, 3.1.3 handling of supporting assets, and 3.1.4 mobile IT devices and mobile data storage devices. Please note: the former 3.1.2 has been superseded. Its content was split into 1.6.3 (crisis management), 5.2.8 (IT service continuity planning) and 5.2.9 (backup and recovery), so this chapter no longer covers 3.1.2 separately. Also, if your assessment scope includes prototype protection, physical security must be combined with the stricter requirements of Chapter 8 (the 8.2 series).

blocks.text: Example security zone classification (based on the examples in the ISA)

head: Typical color
Protection needs
Example areas
rows: Public roads, unfenced parking lots, stairwells in multi-tenant buildings
Fully fenced plant grounds, reception, meeting rooms, corridors
Server rooms, network wiring closets, chemical stores
HR, design department, IT office, management offices

blocks.text: The ISA describes the protection of each zone with four kinds of measures: technical, physical, personnel and organizational. Example for a design room with high protection needs: motion-sensor alarm after working hours; cleaning only during working hours and only with an employee present; no keys handed out to the cleaning company; no photography; access rights reviewed every year; confidential documents locked away after work; visitors escorted at all times.

blocks.title: 3.1.2 has been superseded
blocks.text: In ISA 2027, 3.1.2 is marked "Superseded by 1.6.3, 5.2.8 and 5.2.9". If older documents still refer to 3.1.2, update your mapping table to avoid confusion during the assessment.

Security zones are like an onion: one layer inside the next. Auditors love to look for "holes in the onion", such as the back door of the goods receiving area or the kitchen next to the server room. Check these places with extra care.

controls.title: Management of security zones
controls.q_en: To what extent are security zones managed to protect information assets?
controls.q_zh: To what extent are security zones managed to protect information assets?
controls.objective: Security zones provide physical protection of information assets. The more sensitive the information assets to be processed are the more protective measures are required.

must: A security zone concept including the associated protective measures based on the requirements for the handling of information assets is in place. The following aspects are considered: – Physical conditions (e.g., premises / buildings / spaces) in the definition of security zones; – Delivery and shipping areas.
The defined protective measures are implemented.
The code of conduct for security zones is known to all persons involved.
should: Procedures for allocation and revocation of access rights are established.
Visitor management policies (including registration and escorting of visitors) are defined.
Policies for carrying along and using mobile IT devices and mobile data storage devices (e.g., registration before they are carried along, identification obligations) are defined and implemented.
Network/infrastructure components (own or customer networks) are protected against unauthorized access.
External properties used for storing and processing information assets are considered in the security zone concept (e.g. storage rooms, garages, workshops, test tracks, data processing centres).
high: Protective measures against simple overhearing and viewing are implemented. (C)

controls.refs: ISO 27001:2022 A.7.1–A.7.6 | ISA/IEC 62443-2-1 6.4.1 | NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC-04, PR.AA-06, DE.CM-02, DE.CM-03 | BSI IT-Grundschutz ORP.1, INF.1, INF.2, INF.5–INF.10, OPS.2.1 | NIST SP800-53r5 PE-2, PE-3, PE-6, PE-8, etc.
explain: Security zones are areas arranged in layers, one inside the other, separated by barriers and access control, to protect information assets physically. Think of an onion: the outer layer is the public area, then the plant grounds, then the office area, and at the core the server room or the customer project room. The further in you go, the fewer people may enter and the stricter the controls.

The must requirements have three key points. First, a written security zone concept based on physical conditions (site, buildings, floors, rooms) that explicitly includes the **delivery and shipping areas**, because this is where external people (logistics staff, drivers) come and go most often, and it is the gap most often forgotten. Second, the measures in the concept must really be implemented. Third, all persons involved (including cleaning, security guards and contractors) must know the code of conduct for each zone.

The ISA provides an example of common zone colors: gray public areas (unfenced parking lots, public roads), green normal protection areas (fully fenced plant grounds, reception, meeting rooms, corridors), purple special protection areas (server rooms, network wiring closets, chemical stores), yellow or orange high protection areas (HR, design department, IT office, management offices), and red very high protection areas (customer project offices). The colors are only a convention. What matters is that each zone has matching technical, physical, personnel and organizational measures.

The should requirements cover granting and revoking access rights, visitor registration and escort, rules for bringing in mobile devices, protection of network equipment (for example locked wiring cabinets and disabled unused network ports), and external properties (warehouses, test tracks, external data centers) in the concept. High protection needs (C) require protection against simple overhearing and viewing, for example sound-insulated meeting rooms, frosted film on glass walls and cleaning whiteboards after meetings. Prototype protection has even stricter requirements in the 8.2 series.
practice: Draw a "security zone floor plan" with colors for each protection level, and add a "security zone table" listing for each zone the asset types, who may enter, access control method, monitoring method and code of conduct.

Delivery and shipping areas: set up a receiving area separated from the plant. Drivers may not enter production or office areas. Shipping labels and delivery notes are not left where the public can see them.

Access control: use an access card system with rights set per zone. The zone owner approves requests, rights are revoked on the day of leaving or transfer, and the access list is reviewed every year (at least once a year for high protection zones).

Visitor management: register visitors (name, company, host, time), visitors wear a badge, are escorted at all times in high protection zones, sign a confidentiality statement where necessary, and return the badge when they leave.
Mobile devices and photography: no photography in high protection zones, with signs posted; cover visitors' phone cameras with seal stickers or have phones deposited.
Network and infrastructure: lock server rooms and wiring cabinets, disable unused network ports or enable 802.1X, and keep customer leased-line equipment in a controlled area.
High protection needs: sound insulation for meeting and design rooms, frosted windows or blinds, and screens positioned so they do not face windows or corridors.

questions: Which security zones do you have? How were they designed? Why were they divided this way?
Where are the areas with very high protection needs?
What happens in case of an intrusion?
How many people have access rights to a given zone? Who approved them?
When was the last review of access rights? What was the most recent revocation?
How are the request, approval and issue of access rights recorded?
How does the visitor registration process work?
evidence: Security zone concept and floor plan (site layout)
Key management list
Extract of the electronic access control system's rights list and access logs for specific zones
Visitor management rules and visitor log
Rules for mobile IT devices
Access rights review records
Photos of zones showing the protective measures
Contract with the security company
findings: A security zone floor plan exists, but it does not cover the delivery and shipping areas, and drivers can walk straight into the warehouse and offices.
The security zone concept says there is access control, but on site the server room door is unlocked or kept open with a door wedge.
Access rights have never been reviewed, and access cards of former employees still work.
An external warehouse or test site stores customer parts but is not included in the security zone concept.
Cleaning staff have keys to high protection zones and can enter when nobody is there; this was not assessed in the concept.

controls.tip: Allan's tip: Auditors often walk from the main gate all the way to the server room, comparing your floor plan as they go. Make sure the plan matches reality — do not show an old plan from before the renovation.

controls.title: Handling of supporting assets
controls.q_en: To what extent is the handling of supporting assets managed?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is the handling of supporting assets managed?
controls.objective: During their lifecycle (e.g., usage, disposal), supporting assets are subject to risks such as loss, theft or unauthorized viewing.

must: The requirements for the handling of supporting assets (e.g., transport, storage, repair, loss, return, disposal) are determined and fulfilled.
high: Disposal of supporting assets is conducted in accordance with one of the relevant standards (e.g. ISO 21964, at least security level 4). (C)

explain: Supporting assets are the electronic or physical carriers used to store, process or transmit information assets, for example mobile storage devices, IT systems, IT services and service providers, and paper documents. Information assets are the "content", supporting assets are the "container". At every step — transport, storage, repair, loss, return and disposal — the container can cause the content to leak.

There is only one must requirement, but the six lifecycle steps in brackets are the auditor's checklist: transport (for example sending a hard drive to a customer), storage (confidential documents locked away), repair (is the hard drive removed or encrypted before a laptop is sent to the manufacturer?), loss (reporting process), return (leased equipment, returning devices when leaving) and disposal (destroying hard drives and paper).

High protection needs (C) require disposal according to a standard, for example ISO 21964 (formerly the German DIN 66399), at least security level 4. ISO 21964 classifies by material — for example paper, optical discs, magnetic media, hard drives and electronic storage media — each with a different particle size. If disposal is outsourced, make sure the provider can prove the required level and issues destruction certificates.

Note: in the ISA, the "possible questions" listed under 4.1.1 are actually about supporting assets (for example: what happens to documents when you leave your desk, how are hard drives disposed of, where is the shredder). This course places them under 3.1.3. This control is also related to 1.3.1 asset inventory, 3.1.4 mobile devices, and 5.3.3 return and deletion of data from external IT services.
practice: Create a "supporting asset policy" that defines requirements for transport, storage, repair, loss, return and disposal by asset type (laptops, server hard drives, USB drives, paper, mobile phones, leased multifunction printers).
Define which supporting assets may store which classes of information, for example: confidential data may not be stored on personal USB drives.
Clear desk policy: when leaving the desk or at the end of the day, lock confidential paper documents in a cabinet, lock the screen (Windows+L), and use badge release for printing.
Repair control: before repair, back up and remove or encrypt the storage media; outsourced repairers sign confidentiality clauses; on-site repairs are escorted.

Disposal process: hard drives are degaussed, physically destroyed or wiped with a standard-compliant tool. For high protection needs, follow ISO 21964 at least level 4; outsourced destruction requires a destruction certificate; paper goes into a shredder of the right level or a locked confidential waste bin.
Leased equipment (multifunction printers, laptops): wipe internal hard drives before return, and define the responsibility for data deletion in the lease contract.
For shipping equipment, use encrypted media and trackable logistics, and record sender, recipient and receipt confirmation.

questions: Where have you defined which supporting assets exist and which information assets may be stored on them?
How are supporting assets with high protection needs protected? Which encryption methods are used?
Where are the lifecycle requirements for the different supporting assets documented?
What do employees do with documents when they leave their desk?
How are the hard drives of purchased or leased equipment disposed of?
How are paper documents destroyed? Where are the shredders or confidential waste bins?
evidence: Supporting asset policy
Asset inventory (including supporting assets and the information classes stored)
Disposal records and destruction certificates (including the standard and security level used)
Repair records and confidentiality clauses
Shredder specifications, photos of confidential waste bin locations
Records of data deletion before returning leased equipment
findings: Old computers are handed directly to a recycler without wiping the hard drives and without a destruction certificate.
The shredder cuts only long strips and cannot reach the security level required for high protection needs.
A leased multifunction printer was returned without wiping its internal hard drive, although many confidential drawings had been scanned on it.
A laptop was sent to the manufacturer for repair with an unencrypted hard drive and no confidentiality agreement.

controls.tip: Allan's tip: What I see most often during audits is a "recycling paper box" in the corner of the office, full of price quotations. Replace it with a locked confidential waste bin.

controls.title: Management of mobile IT devices and mobile data storage devices
controls.q_en: To what extent is the handling of mobile IT devices and mobile data storage devices managed?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is the handling of mobile IT devices and mobile data storage devices managed?
controls.objective: Mobile IT devices (e.g., notebooks, tablets, smartphones) and mobile data storage devices (e.g., SD cards, hard drives) are generally used not only on the premises of an organization, but also in mobile applications. This presents an increased risk of loss, theft, etc.

must: The requirements for mobile IT devices and mobile data storage devices are determined and fulfilled. The following aspects are considered: – Encryption; – Access protection (e.g., PIN, password); – Marking (also considering requirements for use in the presence of customers).
should: Registration of the IT devices.
high: General encryption of mobile data storage devices or the information assets stored thereon. Where this is technically not feasible, information is protected by similarly effective measures. (C, I)

explain: 3.1.4 focuses on devices that "travel with you": laptops, tablets and phones, as well as USB flash drives, SD cards and external hard drives. The must requirement asks for three things: encryption, access protection and marking. These must be "determined and fulfilled", so you need written rules and you must be able to show the actual settings on the devices.

Marking has two meanings. First, an asset label, which helps with inventory and with identifying the owner if the device is lost. Second, the original text explicitly mentions requirements for "use in the presence of customers". For example, a laptop with a sticker showing the project name of OEM A, taken to a meeting at OEM B, leaks confidential information. Some OEMs also require that supplier devices used at their sites carry specific markings or are registered. Marking must allow identification without revealing confidential information.

The should requirement asks for device registration, meaning an inventory that shows the custodian, serial number and encryption status of each device. High protection needs (C, I) require **general encryption** of mobile storage devices, for example allowing only hardware-encrypted USB drives or enforcing BitLocker To Go. If some devices (for example the SD card of a measuring instrument) cannot be encrypted for technical reasons, protect them with similarly effective measures, such as using them only inside a security zone, wiping them right after use and keeping them locked away.

This control is related to 2.1.4 mobile work, 3.1.3 supporting assets, 4.1.2 authentication and 5.1.1 cryptography. Common blind spots in factories are USB drives used by production or quality staff to copy programs and measurement data, and development boards and test phones used by R&D. These are also within the scope of mobile devices.
practice: Create a "mobile devices and portable storage media policy": allowed device types, encryption method, PIN and password rules, marking, registration and loss reporting process.
Enforce BitLocker (Windows) or FileVault (macOS) on laptops, report encryption status via Intune or another MDM, and store recovery keys centrally in Entra ID or AD.
Enroll phones and tablets in an MDM (for example Intune or Jamf), enforce screen lock and PIN, and enable remote wipe. For BYOD, use app protection policies to separate company data.
USB control: block unauthorized USB devices with EDR or device control policies and allow only registered encrypted USB drives. For high protection needs, enforce encryption everywhere.

Use neutral numbers on asset labels (for example NB-0123), never customer or project names. Before visiting a customer, check that the wallpaper and login screen do not reveal information about other customers.
Keep a mobile device inventory with serial number, model, custodian, encryption status, MDM enrollment status, and issue and return dates. Check it every six months.

For devices that cannot be encrypted (such as SD cards in measuring equipment), use alternative measures — locked storage, use only in defined areas, wiping after use — and document them in the risk assessment.

questions: Which mobile IT devices and portable storage devices does the company have? Where is the inventory?
Please show the encryption status of one laptop on site, and the overall encryption rate in the MDM report.
How is access protection on phones configured? Can they be wiped remotely if lost?
Can USB flash drives be used freely? How are they controlled?
How are devices marked? Are there special rules for taking them to customer sites?
(High protection needs) What alternative measures are used for storage devices that cannot be encrypted?
evidence: Mobile device policy
Mobile device inventory
MDM or Intune compliance and encryption status reports
Screenshots of USB control policy settings and records of approved exceptions
Photos of asset labels
Loss reports and remote wipe records
findings: Most laptops are encrypted, but several laptops of managers or R&D staff are not encrypted and not registered.
USB use is not controlled at all; production staff copy programs and measurement data with personal flash drives.
Phones can receive company e-mail but are not enrolled in MDM and have no screen lock requirement.
A laptop carries a sticker with a customer project name and is taken to meetings with other customers.

controls.tip: Allan's tip: An encryption rate of 98% sounds good, but the auditor will ask straight away who the remaining 2% are. Prepare the exception list in advance and explain your plan to fix it.

summary: 3.1.1: You need a written security zone concept (including physical conditions and delivery and shipping areas), the measures must be implemented, and all persons involved must know the code of conduct. Should covers granting and revoking access, visitors, mobile devices, network equipment and external properties.
3.1.1 high protection needs: protect against simple overhearing and viewing.

3.1.3: Rules are needed for transport, storage, repair, loss, return and disposal of supporting assets. For high protection needs, disposal follows a standard such as ISO 21964, at least security level 4.

3.1.4: Mobile devices and storage devices must consider encryption, access protection and marking (including use in front of customers). Should: register them. High protection needs: full encryption of mobile storage devices or equivalent measures.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — Identity and Access Management
intro: Chapter 4 is the chapter IT departments know best — and also the one where findings are most common. Identity and access management (IAM) answers three questions: who are you (identification and authentication), how is your account managed (account lifecycle), and what are you allowed to do (access rights). The ISA divides it into 4.1 Identity Management (4.1.1 identification means, 4.1.2 user authentication, 4.1.3 user accounts and login information) and 4.2 Access Management (4.2.1 access rights).

For small and mid-sized suppliers with only a few IT staff, the challenge in this chapter is "making it a process". Accounts, access rights, access cards and tokens are often handled by different people in different ways, without consistent request, approval and review records. We recommend starting with the leaver and transfer processes and connecting HR, facilities and IT into one chain. The main ISA 2027 changes are in 4.1.1 (the time limit for high protection needs was removed) and 4.1.2 (the password requirement became a separate should item, and the wording changed to recognized best practices).
