Question
ISA control
Common tools
rows: What do you use to prove who you are?
Access cards, keys, FIDO keys, smart cards
How do we confirm it is really you?
How is an account created and ended?
AD, Entra ID, HR system integration
What are you allowed to do?

blocks.title: Joiner – Mover – Leaver
blocks.text: In practice, the JML model ties this chapter together. Joiner: create accounts by role and issue identification means. Mover: adjust access rights and remove old ones. Leaver: disable accounts on the last day, collect identification means, and ask customers to disable accounts in customer systems.
I get it now! The account is the "ticket", and the access rights decide "which halls the ticket lets you into". You have to manage both!

controls.title: Management of identification means
controls.q_en: To what extent is the use of identification means managed?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is the use of identification means managed?
controls.objective: To check the authorization for both physical access and electronic access, means of identification such as keys, visual IDs, or other physical access devices, as well as cryptographic tokens are often used. These security features are only reliable if the use of such identification means is handled adequately.

must: The requirements for the handling of identification means over the entire lifecycle are determined and fulfilled. The following aspects are considered: – Creation, handover, return and destruction; – Validity periods; – Traceability; – Handling of loss.
should: Identification means can be produced under controlled conditions only.
high: A strategy of blocking or invalidation of identification means in case of loss is prepared and implemented as far as possible. (C, I, A)

controls.refs: ISO 27001:2022 A.5.18 | NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AA-01 | BSI IT-Grundschutz SYS.4.5, SYS.3.1, SYS.3.2.1, SYS.3.3 | NIST SP800-53r5 SC-41, SC-42
controls.change2027: ISA 2027 removed the high protection needs requirement that identification means must be time-limited. Validity periods are still one of the aspects to consider in the must requirement.
explain: Identification means include physical and electronic items: physical keys, access cards, employee badges and visitor badges, as well as smart cards, hardware tokens, FIDO2 security keys and OTP generators. They show that "the holder is allowed in". If their management gets out of control, access control and MFA become useless.

The must requirement asks you to manage the entire lifecycle and lists four aspects: creation, handover, return and destruction; validity periods (for example visitor badges valid for one day, contractor access cards valid for the contract period); traceability (you know which card or key is held by whom); and handling of loss (reporting, blocking, reissue).

The should requirement says identification means may only be produced under controlled conditions, for example access cards issued in the system by facilities, the card printer locked away and blank cards counted; keys of a patented system that cannot be copied without authorization. High protection needs (C, I, A) require a prepared strategy to block or invalidate identification means when lost, for example blocking an access card immediately in the system or revoking a security key in Entra ID. For traditional keys that cannot be disabled remotely, the strategy may be to replace the lock cylinder.

ISA 2027 removed the "time limit" requirement for high protection needs, but validity periods are still an aspect of the must requirement, so you still need to define validity periods for each type of identification means. This control is closely related to 3.1.1 access rights, 4.1.3 account management and the leaver process: when people leave, badges, keys and tokens must be returned and disabled in the system at the same time.
practice: Create an "identification means register": type (key, access card, badge, token, FIDO key), number, holder, issue date, validity period, return date.

Facilities or the security team issue identification means centrally; the card printer and blank cards are locked away. Use patented keys that cannot be copied freely; copies require an approved request.
Visitor badges are collected every day; contractor access cards get an expiry date and stop working automatically; employee card rights are adjusted when the person's job changes.

Handling of loss: employees report a loss immediately; the access card is blocked in the system right away; tokens or FIDO keys are revoked in the identity system and re-enrolled; if a key to an important area is lost, assess replacing the lock cylinder.
Add a "return of identification means" field to the leaver form, completed on the same day as account deactivation and signed off by facilities.
Damaged or collected cards and tokens are physically destroyed, and the destruction is recorded.
Check the register once a year against the staff list and the access control system.

questions: Which identification means does the company use? Who issues and manages them?
Where are the records of issuing, returning and destroying access cards and keys?
How are the validity periods of visitor badges and contractor access cards set?
Please describe how the most recent loss of an identification means was handled.
How are blank access cards and card printers stored? Can keys be copied freely?
(High protection needs) How are lost identification means blocked or invalidated? How fast?
evidence: Identification means policy and register
Access card issue and deactivation records (reports from the access control system)
Key issue and return log
Loss reports and blocking records
Return records for identification means on leaver forms
Token or FIDO key enrollment and revocation records
findings: Departments have keys cut on their own; facilities does not know how many keys exist or who holds them.
A former employee did not return the badge, and the access card still opens the plant gate.
Visitor badges are not numbered and not collected, so anyone who has one can get in.
An employee reported a lost access card only a week later; the card remained active during that time and nobody followed up.

controls.tip: Allan's tip: During a consulting job I once asked facilities "How many keys are there to the server room?" The answer was "Probably three." In the end we found seven. Start building your register today.

controls.title: Secure user access to IT services and IT systems
controls.q_en: To what extent is the user access to IT services and IT systems secured?
controls.q_zh: To what extent is the user access to IT services and IT systems secured?
controls.objective: Only securely identified (authenticated) users are to gain access to IT systems. For this purpose, the identity of a user is securely determined by suitable procedures.

must: The procedures for user authentication are selected based on a risk assessment. Possible attack scenarios are considered (e.g., direct accessibility via the internet).
Authentication procedures are consistent with recognized security best practices.
should: The user authentication procedures are defined and implemented based on the business-related and security-relevant requirements.
Users are authenticated at least by means of strong passwords according to proven and widely accepted practices.
Superior procedures are used for the authentication of privileged user accounts (e.g., privileged access management, two-factor authentication).
high: Depending on the risk assessment, authentication procedure and access control have been enhanced by supplementary measures (e.g., continuous access monitoring with respect to irregularities or use of strong authentication, automatic logout, disabling in case of inactivity, or brute force prevention). (C, I, A)
vhigh: Before gaining access to data of very high protection needs, users are authenticated by means of strong authentication (e.g., two-factor authentication) (C, I)

controls.refs: ISO 27001:2022 A.5.15, A.8.5 | NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AA-02, PR.AA-03 | BSI IT-Grundschutz ORP.4, OPS.1.1.2 | NIST SP800-53r5 AC-2(12), AC-3(14), AC-7, AC-11, AC-12, AC-17, IA-5, IA-11, etc.
controls.change2027: ISA 2027 changed the should item on "passwords according to the state of the art" from a sub-point (–) to a separate requirement (+). ISA 2027.1 also replaced the term "state-of-the-art" with "proven and widely accepted practices" and "recognized security best practices".
explain: 4.1.2 answers the question: when a user logs in, how do you know it is really that person? The must requirement does not say directly whether to use passwords or MFA. Instead it asks for two things: the authentication method is chosen based on a **risk assessment** that considers attack scenarios, such as systems directly reachable from the internet (VPN, webmail, M365, remote desktop); and the method is consistent with recognized security best practices.

In other words, if your M365 is open to the internet and uses only passwords, it is hard to show that you considered internet attack scenarios and follow best practices. Note: commonly cited best practices include NIST SP 800-63B and BSI recommendations. Today's mainstream view focuses on password length and checking against leaked passwords, rather than forcing frequent changes. ISA 2027.1 deliberately changed "state-of-the-art" to "proven and widely accepted", so organizations can use such recognized standards as their basis.

The should requirements: define authentication procedures based on business and security requirements, use at least strong passwords, and use superior methods (PAM, 2FA) for privileged accounts. High protection needs (C, I, A) add supplementary measures depending on risk, such as monitoring for unusual logins, automatic logout, disabling after inactivity, account lockout or brute-force protection. Very high protection needs (C, I) require strong authentication, for example two-factor authentication, before accessing data with very high protection needs.

A common misunderstanding is "we have MFA, so we are done". Auditors will ask: which systems have MFA? What about OT systems, local server administrators, network devices and cloud consoles? How are service accounts handled? The choice of authentication method must be supported by a documented risk assessment and should be looked at together with 4.1.3 account management and 4.2.1 access rights management.
practice: Create a "system authentication overview": for each system (AD, M365, VPN, ERP, MES, PLM, firewall, cloud console), whether it is internet-facing, its protection needs, the authentication method used, whether MFA is used, and the risk assessment basis.
Enable MFA for all internet-facing services (M365, VPN, remote access). Prefer authenticator push with number matching or FIDO2, and avoid SMS-only methods.

Base the password policy on recognized practice, for example a minimum length of 12 characters or more, blocking common and leaked passwords (Entra Password Protection), and an account lockout threshold.

Privileged accounts: administrators use separate privileged accounts with mandatory MFA; critical systems use PAM (for example CyberArk, Delinea, or LAPS plus a jump server); privileged sessions are recorded or logged.

Supplementary measures for high protection needs: conditional access (only compliant devices, block logins from high-risk countries), alerts on unusual logins sent to the SIEM, automatic screen lock after 10–15 minutes of inactivity, and automatic logout from applications when idle.
For data with very high protection needs (for example customer project folders or confidential PLM projects), enforce MFA or a dedicated environment before access.
Once a year, check whether the authentication methods still meet best practices, and document this in the management review or risk assessment.

questions: Which user authentication methods does the organization use?
What is the basis for choosing the authentication methods (risk assessment, best practices, business and security requirements)?
Which methods are used to authenticate privileged user accounts?
How do you make sure the password standard used by the organization matches current best practices?
Have sensitive resources been identified? Which sensitive resources and systems are accessed with two-factor authentication?
How do you make sure privileged access rights are restricted, controlled and protected by stronger authentication?
Has information with very high protection needs been identified, and is access to it protected with a second factor?
evidence: Risk assessment of authentication methods or the system authentication overview
Password policy and screenshots of AD or Entra ID password settings
MFA enrollment status report and conditional access policies
PAM system configuration and list of privileged accounts
Screenshots of account lockout and idle logout settings
Records of alerts on unusual logins
findings: VPN and webmail are open to the internet with username and password only, and no risk assessment was done.
Normal users have MFA, but domain administrator and firewall administrator accounts do not.
The password policy requires only 6 characters, which does not match recognized best practices.
Data with very high protection needs has not been identified, so nobody can explain which access requires a second factor.
There is no record of why the authentication methods were chosen; the only answer is "that is the vendor default".

controls.tip: Allan's tip: The places where MFA is most often missing are "administrators" and "network devices", because everyone thinks IT's own people will not cause problems. But these are exactly the accounts hackers want most.

controls.title: Secure management of user accounts and login information
controls.q_en: To what extent are user accounts and login information securely managed and applied?
controls.q_zh: To what extent are user accounts and login information securely managed and applied?
controls.objective: Access to information and IT systems is provided via validated user accounts assigned to a person. It is important to protect login information and to ensure the traceability of transactions and accesses.

must: The creating, changing, and deleting of user accounts is conducted.
Unique and personalized user accounts are used.
The use of “shared accounts” is regulated (e.g., restricted to cases where traceability of actions is dispensable).
User accounts are disabled immediately after the user has resigned from or left the organization (e.g., upon termination of the employment contract).
User accounts are regularly reviewed.
The login information is provided to the user in a secure manner.

A policy for the handling of login information is defined and implemented. The following aspects are considered: – No disclosure of login information, not even to persons of authority, within the limits of applicable law; – No writing down or unencrypted storing of login information; – Immediate changing of login information whenever potential compromising is suspected; – No use of identical login information for business and non-business purposes; – Changing of temporary or initial login information following the 1st login; – Requirements for the quality of authentication information (e.g., length of password, types of characters to be used).
should: A basic user account with minimum access rights and functionalities is existent and used.
Default accounts and passwords pre-configured by manufacturers are disabled (e.g., by blocking or changing of password).
User accounts are created or authorized by the responsible body.
Creating user accounts is subject to an approval process (four-eyes principle).
User accounts of service providers are disabled upon completion of their task.
Deadlines for disabling and deleting user accounts are defined.
The use of default passwords is technically prevented.
Where strong authentication is applied, the use of the medium (e.g., ownership factor) is secure.
User accounts are reviewed at regular intervals. This also includes user accounts in customers' IT systems.
Interactive login for service accounts (technical accounts) is technically prevented.

controls.refs: ISO 27001:2022 A.5.16, A.5.17, A.5.18, A.8.9 | NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AA-04 | BSI IT-Grundschutz ORP.4, OPS.1.1.2 | NIST SP800-53r5 AC-2(2), IA-2, IA-4, IA-5(13), IA-6, IA-7, IA-8, IA-11, AC-16, AC-20, CA-9, SC-2
explain: 4.1.3 has the most must requirements in Chapter 4. The core idea is **one person, one account; every account has a lifecycle; passwords follow rules**. Accounts must be unique and personal so you can trace "who did what". Shared accounts may only be used where traceability is not needed, and must be regulated, for example a read-only account on a production dashboard PC.

Lifecycle: creating, changing and deleting accounts needs a process. Leaver accounts must be disabled "immediately". This is the item auditors check most often, usually by comparing the list of leavers with the deactivation dates in AD or M365. Accounts must be reviewed regularly. Initial passwords must be delivered securely, for example in person, through separate channels or with a one-time link — never written in an e-mail to the manager to pass on.

The login information policy must cover six points: no disclosure (not even to managers or IT), no writing down or unencrypted storage (for example sticky notes or plain-text Excel files), immediate change if a leak is suspected, no use of the same password for business and private purposes, change of the initial password at first login, and password quality requirements. These six points are usually written in a "password management policy" and made known to employees through the 2.1.3 training.

The ten should requirements are worth checking one by one. Items often overlooked are: manufacturer default accounts (for example admin/admin on network devices, printers, PLCs and IP cameras), disabling service provider accounts when their task is finished, reviewing accounts in customer IT systems (for example an employee's account on an OEM supplier portal — when the employee leaves, the customer must be asked to disable it), and technically preventing interactive login for service accounts.
practice: Create an "account management procedure": request, approval (requester's manager plus system owner, four-eyes principle), creation, change, deactivation and deletion. Define deadlines for deactivation (for example disabled on the last day, deleted after 90 days).
Integrate the HR system with AD or Entra ID, or let the leaver form trigger same-day deactivation by IT. Every month, compare the HR leaver list with account status.
Shared account register: purpose, users, why traceability is not needed, and compensating measures (for example read-only, limited to specific terminals), approved by the security officer.
Generate initial passwords randomly, deliver them through separate channels (for example the account name by e-mail and the password by text message), and force a change at first login.
Create a "password and login information policy" that covers the six must points, and roll out a company-approved password manager (for example Bitwarden, 1Password or Keeper).
Add "change or disable default accounts and passwords" to the checklist for commissioning new equipment, including OT devices, network devices, printers and IP cameras.
For service accounts, use GPO settings "Deny log on locally" and "Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services", or use gMSA.
Review accounts every six months (including customer portals and supplier remote maintenance accounts); the system owner signs off the review records.

questions: How are user accounts created, changed, blocked and deleted? Are unique, personal accounts used?
What security measures are in place where shared accounts are used?
Are user accounts reviewed regularly? Can you show the most recent review record?
How is login information delivered to users?
Which rules for handling login information have been defined and implemented?
What training have employees received on handling login information?
What security considerations ensure that login information is not disclosed?
Please compare last month's leaver list with the AD account deactivation dates.
evidence: Account management procedure and account request forms (with approval records)
AD or Entra ID account list and last-logon report
Comparison of the leaver list with account deactivation dates
Shared account register and approval records
Password and login information policy
Account review records (including accounts in customer systems)
GPO settings that prevent interactive login for service accounts
findings: Accounts of former employees were still active several weeks after they left, and some even show logins.
Production and quality staff log in to the MES with shared accounts that can change data; the operator cannot be traced, and this is not regulated.
IT sends initial passwords in plain text by e-mail and does not force a change at first login.
Network switches and PLCs still use factory default passwords.
Employee accounts on customer portals have never been reviewed, and former employees can still log in to customer systems.

controls.tip: Allan's tip: When I worked as an auditor, leaver account deactivation was the check with the highest hit rate. Ask IT to compare the list with HR once a month. It takes ten minutes and can save you a finding.

controls.title: Assignment and management of access rights
controls.q_en: To what extent are access rights assigned and managed?
controls.q_zh: To what extent are access rights assigned and managed?
controls.objective: The management of access rights ensures that only authorized users have access to information and IT services. For this purpose, access rights are assigned to user accounts.

must: The requirements for the management of access rights (authorization) are determined and fulfilled. The following aspects are considered: – Procedure for application, verification, and approval; – Applying the minimum (“need-to-know”/"least privilege") principle; – Access rights are revoked when no longer needed.
The access rights granted for normal and privileged user accounts and technical accounts are reviewed at regular intervals also within IT systems of customers.
should: Strategies for authorizing access to information are prepared.
Authorization roles are used.
Rights are allocated on a need-to-use basis and according to the role and/or area of responsibility.
Normal user accounts are not granted privileged access rights.
The user’s access rights are updated after the user’s responsibilities have changed (e.g., to another field of responsibility).
high: The access rights are approved by the responsible internal Information Officer. (C, I, A)
vhigh: Information is stored in encrypted form at content level (e.g., file level) to prevent unauthorized persons from gaining access and information (privileged users). Where encryption is not feasible, information shall be protected by similarly effective measures. (C)
Existing access rights are regularly reviewed at shorter intervals (e.g., quarterly). (C)

explain: 4.1.3 manages the "account"; 4.2.1 manages "what the account can do". The must requirement asks for a process for requesting, verifying and approving access rights, following the minimum principle (need-to-know and least privilege), and revoking rights when they are no longer needed. The rights of normal, privileged and technical accounts must be reviewed regularly — including the rights in customer IT systems.

The should requirements recommend managing rights with **roles** (RBAC), for example a "sales assistant" role that can view orders in the ERP but cannot change prices; allocating rights on a need-to-use basis and by responsibility; not giving privileged rights to normal accounts (for example the everyday account should not be a local administrator); and updating rights when people change jobs, to avoid "privilege creep" — the longer someone stays and the more departments they move through, the more rights they collect.

High protection needs (C, I, A) require approval of access rights by the responsible internal information officer, meaning the owner of the information (for example the project manager or the head of design) agrees — not IT deciding on its own. Very high protection needs (C) add two items: information is encrypted at content level so that even IT administrators cannot see the content, for example with Microsoft Purview sensitivity label encryption or encrypted containers; and access rights are reviewed at shorter intervals (for example quarterly).

A common mistake is to turn the "access review" into IT printing a list and stamping it. An effective review is done by the information owner or the department manager, who confirms "do these people still need these rights?" Rights that are no longer needed are actually removed, and this is recorded. This control supports and is supported by 1.3.2 information classification, 4.1.3 account management and 5.2.4 log monitoring.
practice: Create an "access rights management procedure" that defines the fields of the request form (requester, system, role, reason, duration, manager approval, information owner approval, IT execution).
Build a "role and rights matrix": define standard roles by department and job for the file server, ERP, PLM, MES and M365 SharePoint. New hires get rights based on their role.
Grant rights on file servers and SharePoint through AD groups, not to individuals directly. The project manager is the owner of each project folder.
Administrators use separate privileged accounts, and local administrator rights are removed from everyday accounts (for example with LAPS or Intune Endpoint Privilege Management).
Transfer process: HR sends a transfer notice, and IT resets rights for the new role and removes the old rights.

Access reviews: normal systems every six or twelve months, privileged accounts every quarter. The information owner confirms and signs off, and removals are recorded. Include employee rights in customer systems (such as OEM portals and customer VPNs).

Very high protection needs: use Purview sensitivity labels or file encryption tools for content-level encryption, restrict privileged administrators from accessing content, and review rights every quarter.

questions: What is the process for requesting, verifying and approving access rights? Please show three sampled request records.
How do you implement the least privilege principle? Is there a role and rights matrix?
When an employee changes jobs, how are the rights from the old department removed?
When was the last access review? Who did it? How were the issues found handled?
Are the rights of privileged and service accounts included in the review? What about rights in customer systems?
(High protection needs) Are access rights approved by the information owner?
(Very high protection needs) How do you prevent IT administrators from seeing the content of strictly confidential data?
evidence: Access rights management procedure and request forms
Role and rights matrix
AD group membership reports, file server permission reports
Access review records and records of removals
Records of rights changes after transfers
Content-level encryption configuration (such as sensitivity label policies)
Review records for account rights in customer systems
findings: Access rights are requested only verbally or by chat message (for example WhatsApp, LINE or Teams); there are no formal request and approval records.
Many folders on the file server are shared with Everyone or Domain Users, which violates the least privilege principle.
Employees keep the rights of their old department after a transfer, leading to privilege creep.
Access reviews are done by IT alone, without confirmation by the information owners, and do not cover service accounts or customer systems.
Everyday user accounts have domain administrator rights.

controls.tip: Allan's tip: "Everyone" in folder permissions is an auditor's favorite. Before the assessment, scan the file server permissions with a tool. You will get a shock — but better now than during the assessment.

summary: 4.1.1: Identification means (keys, access cards, tokens) need full lifecycle management: creation, handover, return and destruction, validity periods, traceability and handling of loss. For high protection needs, have a strategy to block or invalidate them when lost.

4.1.2: Choose authentication methods based on a risk assessment, consider internet attack scenarios, and follow recognized best practices. Use PAM or 2FA for privileged accounts. High: add monitoring, automatic logout and brute-force protection. Very high: strong authentication before access.

4.1.3: One person, one account; rules for shared accounts; immediate deactivation when people leave; regular reviews; secure delivery of initial passwords; a login information policy with six points. Should covers default passwords, the four-eyes principle, no interactive login for service accounts, and reviews of accounts in customer systems.

4.2.1: Access rights need a request, review and approval process, least privilege, revocation when no longer needed, and regular reviews (including privileged and technical accounts and customer systems). High: approval by the information owner. Very high: content-level encryption and quarterly reviews.
Most common findings: leaver accounts not disabled, no MFA for administrators, shared accounts without traceability, folders shared with Everyone, and access reviews done only on paper.

lines.text: Hello everyone! Today we start ISA Chapter 2, Human Resources. Allan, why does a security standard care about HR topics at all?
Because no firewall in the world can stop a person who emails drawings to a private mailbox. In the end, information security is really about managing people.
Chapter 2 follows the employee lifecycle: before joining, when signing the contract, during employment, and when people work outside the office.
So let's start with 2.1.1. The question is about ensuring the qualification of employees in sensitive work fields. What is a sensitive work field?
It is a job where the wrong person could cause a serious security risk. Think of system administrators, R&D and design, HR and payroll, finance, and people who handle prototypes.

slide.title: 2.1.1 Three must requirements
bullets: Identify sensitive work fields and jobs
Define and meet job profile requirements
Verify the identity of potential employees

lines.text: There are three must requirements, and they form a chain. First decide which jobs are sensitive, then write the requirements into the job description, and when hiring, at least check the ID.
Wow, checking the ID counts too? Isn't that something everyone does anyway?
They do it, but there is no record! I once helped a factory where HR said they check every ID. I asked where the record was, and she pointed at her head and said, right here.
Ha ha, I don't think auditors accept records stored in someone's head!
Exactly. So just add a field to the onboarding checklist: ID checked, by whom, and the date. No need for a big pile of ID copies. That would actually create a privacy risk.
And what about the should part? How deep should we check people for sensitive jobs?

slide.title: 2.1.1 Should
bullets: Normal jobs: interview to check suitability
Depth of checks depends on the job

lines.text: Should has two levels. For most people, a simple method like an interview. For sensitive jobs, extended checks, such as calling former employers, verifying diplomas, or even asking for a police certificate.
But wait, could checks like that break data protection law in some countries?

Good question! In practice you need the person's consent, and you only check what is relevant to the job. HR and legal should write a check list for sensitive jobs: what is checked, and which consent is needed.
And don't forget agency workers and contract engineers on site. In the contract, require the agency to do equivalent checks and give you a written declaration.
Note this down! Sensitive jobs need a list, checks need consent forms, and external staff are covered by contracts.
Next is 2.1.2. All staff must be contractually bound to comply with the security policies.

slide.title: 2.1.2 Must and should
bullets: Must: obligation to comply with IS policies
Should: security in contracts, violation procedure

lines.text: Everyone, please circle this. The control question says all staff. That means permanent staff, agency workers, interns, student workers, and anyone working on site long-term.
There are only two must requirements: the non-disclosure obligation and the obligation to follow the security policies. Both must be in effect, which means signed, dated, and matching the staff list.
And the should item says confidentiality must go beyond the employment contract. What does that mean?

It means people must keep secrets even after they leave. A common setup is the employment contract plus a confidentiality agreement plus the work rules. The agreement sets how long it lasts after leaving.

One more thing. Trade secret law usually protects you only if the company took reasonable measures to keep things secret. Signed confidentiality agreements are key evidence. Two wins for one signature.
Wow, so a confidentiality agreement is not just for TISAX. It is also a legal weapon to protect the company!
Right. You also need a procedure for violations, so employees know the consequences. Ideally it is linked to the disciplinary rules in your work rules.
So how do auditors check these two controls? Any tricks we should know?

slide.title: How auditors check
bullets: Pick random names from the staff list
Ask about agency workers and interns
Ask for examples of handled violations

lines.text: The classic method is to pick three random people from the staff list and ask for their signed records. If they pick an agency worker or someone who just became permanent, the paper is often missing.
I saw this myself as an auditor. All permanent staff were fine, then I picked an intern, and HR suddenly realized that interns had never signed anything.
Oh no, that is an instant finding. What a pity.
So my advice is: once a year, check the staff list yourself and confirm one hundred percent of people have signed. It does not take long.
Let's sum up! 2.1.1: identify sensitive jobs first, always check identity, and extended checks depend on risk. 2.1.2: everyone signs confidentiality and compliance, ideally valid after they leave.
In the next part we talk about training and working from home. That is a real headache for many companies right now!

slide.title: Key points
bullets: Sensitive jobs list and ID check records

lines.text: Welcome back! This part covers 2.1.3, security training, and 2.1.4, mobile work. Allan, isn't one training class per year enough?

slide.title: 2.1.3 Awareness and training
bullets: Must: employees trained and made aware

lines.text: If you only do one class per year, you pass the must requirement, but your maturity level will probably stay very basic.
The must requirement is just one sentence: employees are trained and aware. But to reach maturity level 3, you need the six should items.
First, you need a training concept that covers seven topics. Auditors often compare these seven topics one by one with the table of contents of your training material.

slide.title: Seven topics of the training concept
bullets: Malware response, account and password rules

lines.text: External IT services need training too? Do you mean the cloud?
Yes, like free cloud storage, online translation, and generative AI tools. Many engineers paste a specification into a translator, and the data is gone. You must train people on this.
Wow, that is really common. I know people who do exactly that!
Second, target groups. ISA 2027 puts special focus on management, including top leadership. Also system administrators, people with access to customer networks, and production staff.

slide.title: ISA 2027 target groups
bullets: Employees with access to customer networks

lines.text: Why does the boss need special training? Doesn't the boss know best?
Because bosses are the favorite target of fraudsters. A fake boss asks accounting to transfer money, a fake customer changes the bank account. This kind of social engineering aims at managers.
Production staff are different too. They may have no computer and no email. A five-minute talk in the shift meeting, posters, or short videos work much better.
And the other should items? What else do we need?
Management must approve the training concept. Training happens regularly and also after events. Attendance is recorded. And employees must know who their security contact is.
During audits I often ask random employees who they would call if their computer had a virus. Some people say: the colleague next to me who is good with computers.
Ha ha ha, that poor colleague is so busy. He should get a security bonus!
So put the security contact on notice boards, on the intranet home page, even on the desktop wallpaper. And run a phishing test every quarter, with extra training for anyone who clicks.
Note this down! A concept, target groups, approval, regular and event-driven training, records, and a known contact.
Next is 2.1.4, mobile work. Since the pandemic, everyone is used to working from home.

slide.title: 2.1.4 Five must aspects
bullets: Secure handling of electronic and paper info
Theft protection, secure access to IT

lines.text: ISA 2027 rewrote this must requirement and lists five aspects: private surroundings, public surroundings, secure handling of information, theft protection, and secure access to company IT services.
ISA 2027.1 also adds a definition of a coworking space. It is a shared office provided by a third party that is not part of your ISMS. So it is not one of your security zones.
And for handling information, what should we watch out for?

The text says you must consider protection needs and contract requirements, and that includes paper. Some OEM contracts say drawings may only be handled on company premises. Your home office rules must say that.
I once saw an R&D engineer take a whole stack of drawings home, read them, and then throw them into the neighborhood recycling bin. If the customer found out, that would be very serious.
Oh my, the recycling bin became a data leak channel.
On the technical side: full-disk encryption on laptops, VPN or ZTNA with MFA, and Intune checking that the device is compliant before it can connect.

slide.title: Mobile work in practice
bullets: High protection: privacy filter and headset

lines.text: And what about should and high protection needs?

Should mentions that authorities may inspect devices when you travel, and measures for high-risk countries. Many big companies give out clean travel laptops and let people carry only the data they need.

High protection needs mean protection against overhearing and viewing. Opening customer drawings on a train or talking loudly about a project in a cafe are bad examples. Privacy filters are cheap. Hand them out.
How will the auditor ask about mobile work?
First the auditor asks if you allow working from home, then wants to see the written rules. If you say no, but the VPN log shows someone connecting at ten at night, that is awkward.
Ha ha, caught by the connection log. No excuses possible!
Let's sum up! 2.1.3: training needs a plan, target groups, and records. 2.1.4: mobile work covers private and public surroundings, paper and electronic data, theft protection, and secure connections.
In the next chapter we walk into the plant and see how security zones are set up. Allan says he will explain it with an onion. Stay tuned!
Hello everyone! Today we start Chapter 3, Physical Security. Allan, last time you promised to explain security zones with an onion. I am ready!
Did you bring an onion? First a quick reminder: 3.1.2 has been superseded. Its content moved to 1.6.3 crisis management, 5.2.8 IT service continuity, and 5.2.9 backup.
So if old documents still mention 3.1.2, we need to update the mapping table.

Exactly. OK, back to the onion. Security zones are layers wrapped around each other. Everyone can reach the outer layer. The further in you go, the fewer people may enter and the stricter the controls.

slide.title: Security zones are like an onion
bullets: Inner layers: server room, design room

lines.text: The ISA even gives color examples: gray for public, green for normal, purple for special, yellow or orange for high protection, and red for very high protection.

head: Color
Examples
rows: Server room, wiring closet, chemical store

lines.text: Wow, the server room is purple, not the top level red?

In the example, the server room has special protection needs. That is the convention in the ISA. But the color is not the point. The point is which measures you define for each zone, and that you really apply them.
So what does the 3.1.1 must requirement ask for?

slide.title: 3.1.1 Must
bullets: Physical conditions, delivery and shipping areas
Everyone involved knows the code of conduct

lines.text: Three things. First, a security zone concept, divided by site, buildings and spaces, with special attention to the delivery and shipping areas.
Why does the text name the delivery and shipping areas specifically?
Because that is the hole in the onion! Drivers come and go all day. I have seen many plants where the back door of the receiving area leads straight into the offices, with no separation at all.
Second, the measures must be implemented. Third, everyone involved must know the code of conduct, including cleaning staff, security guards, and contractors.
Even the cleaning staff need to know the code of conduct?
Of course. The ISA example says that in a design room with high protection needs, cleaners may only work during office hours with an employee present, and the cleaning company gets no keys.
I see! In normal areas, the cleaning company can have keys and clean at night, but not in high protection areas.
The should part has five items. Let me list them for everyone.

slide.title: 3.1.1 Should
bullets: Process to grant and revoke access rights
Rules for bringing and using mobile devices
Protect network gear, include external sites

lines.text: Access needs a process for granting and revoking rights. Visitors must be registered and escorted. Mobile devices brought in need rules, for example registration or a photo ban.

Network and infrastructure components must be protected too. Lock the wiring cabinet in the corridor, disable unused network ports in meeting rooms, and keep customer line equipment in a controlled area.
Many people forget the last item: external properties. A rented warehouse, a test track, an external data center. If your information assets are there, include them in the concept.
Like suppliers who keep customer samples in a rented warehouse. Does that count?
It counts. And if they are prototypes, the stricter requirements of Chapter 8 also apply. We will cover that in the prototype protection module.
And for high protection needs, what do we add?
Protection against simple overhearing and viewing. Poor sound insulation in meeting rooms, design room windows facing the corridor, whiteboards not wiped after meetings. These are common problems.
Once I was waiting in a customer's corridor and could read the prices on the whiteboard in the next meeting room through the glass. Of course, being very professional, I looked away.
Ha ha, lucky it was you, Allan, and not a competitor!
When the auditor comes on site, how will they check the security zones?

slide.title: How auditors check on site
bullets: Walk from the gate to the server room with the plan
Ask how many people have access to a zone

lines.text: They walk around with your floor plan and compare as they go. They ask how many people have access to a zone, who approved it, when the last review was, and what the most recent revocation was.
The most common findings are a floor plan that does not match reality, or a server room door held open with a wedge because it is too hot inside.
If the server room door is wedged open, the lock is pointless.
Another common finding is access cards of former employees that still work. We will look at that in detail in Chapter 4, identification means.
Key points! Security zones are like an onion. You need a concept, the measures must be in place, and everyone must know the rules. Don't forget delivery areas and external properties.
In the next part we talk about supporting assets and mobile devices, from shredders to USB flash drives. Don't go away!

slide.title: Key points
bullets: Zone concept incl. delivery and shipping
Measures in place, code of conduct known

lines.text: Welcome back! This part is about 3.1.3 supporting assets and 3.1.4 mobile devices. Allan, supporting assets sounds so abstract.

slide.title: 3.1.3 Supporting assets
bullets: Carriers that store, process, transmit info
Electronic: hard drives, USB, IT systems

lines.text: Let me use a comparison. Information assets are the drink, supporting assets are the cup. If the cup breaks, is taken away, or is sent for repair, the drink can spill.
So supporting assets are the cups that hold the information!
Right. There is only one must requirement: define and fulfill requirements for handling supporting assets. In brackets, it lists six lifecycle steps.

slide.title: 3.1.3 Must: six steps
bullets: High: dispose per ISO 21964, level 4 or above

lines.text: Transport, storage, repair, loss, return, disposal. These six words are the auditor's checklist, and they will ask you about each one.
Repair too? Isn't that the vendor's job?
Of course. A laptop goes for repair with an unencrypted drive full of customer drawings. Or a leased printer is returned with its internal drive full of scanned confidential documents.
Wow, printers have hard drives? I had no idea!
Many people don't know. So the lease contract should say data is deleted before return, and ideally the vendor gives you a deletion record.
And high protection needs say disposal follows ISO 21964. What is that?

ISO 21964 is the international standard for destroying data carriers. It came from the German DIN 66399. It is organized by material, and paper, hard drives and electronic media each have their own particle size levels.
High protection needs require at least security level 4. For paper, a normal strip-cut shredder usually does not reach that. Use a fine particle-cut shredder, or a certified destruction company.
Note this down! For outsourced destruction, get a destruction certificate that states the standard and the security level.
What I see most often during audits is a box in the office corner labeled recycling paper, full of price quotations. Please replace it with a locked confidential waste bin.
The possible questions in the ISA also ask what employees do with documents when they leave their desk.
Yes, that is clear desk and screen lock. Press Windows plus L when you leave your desk, lock confidential documents in a drawer after work, and use badge release for printing.
Next is 3.1.4, mobile IT devices and mobile data storage devices.

slide.title: 3.1.4 Must: three elements
bullets: Marking, incl. use in front of customers

lines.text: Things you carry around have the highest risk: laptops, tablets, phones, and also USB drives, SD cards, and external hard drives. The must requirement asks for three things: encryption, access protection, and marking.
I understand encryption and passwords. But what does marking mean?
Marking has two meanings. One is the asset label, which helps with inventory. The other is that the ISA explicitly asks you to consider use in front of customers.
I once saw a salesperson whose laptop had a sticker with the project code of OEM A, and he took it to a meeting at OEM B. The buyer at OEM B kept staring at that sticker.
Ha ha, how embarrassing. That is like giving a presentation for the competitor!
So use neutral numbers on asset labels, like NB-0123. Before you visit a customer, also check your wallpaper and recently opened files, so you don't show other customers' information.
And for high protection needs, what do we add?

Mobile storage devices or the data on them must be fully encrypted. Where that is not technically possible, use equally effective measures, such as locked storage, use only in defined areas, and wiping after use.
In practice, laptops use BitLocker or FileVault, and Intune reports the encryption rate. For USB, use device control in your EDR and allow only registered, encrypted flash drives.
What about SD cards in measuring instruments in the plant? Those probably can't be encrypted.
Good question! That is a case for alternative measures. Document it in the risk assessment: explain why it cannot be encrypted and how you compensate.
One more audit tip: if you say your encryption rate is 98 percent, the auditor will definitely ask which devices are the other 2 percent. Have the exception list ready.
Usually that 2 percent is the boss's laptop, right...
You got it! That is why the senior management training we talked about earlier is so important.
Chapter 3 summary! Security zones are like an onion. Manage the six steps for supporting assets and follow a standard for disposal. Mobile devices need encryption, passwords, and smart marking.

slide.title: Chapter 3 summary
bullets: Supporting assets: six steps, standard disposal
Next chapter: identity and access management

lines.text: The next chapter is identity and access management. IT colleagues know it best, and it is also where findings are most common. See you in the next part!
Hello everyone! We are now in Chapter 4, Identity and Access Management. Allan says this is where IT gets the most findings. I am so nervous!
Don't worry. This chapter answers three questions: who are you, how is your account managed, and what are you allowed to do. Let's start with 4.1.1, identification means.
What exactly are identification means? It sounds very broad.
Keys, access cards, employee badges, visitor badges, and electronic ones like smart cards, hardware tokens, and FIDO security keys. Anything used to prove who you are.

slide.title: 4.1.1 Identification means
bullets: Electronic: tokens, smart cards, FIDO keys

lines.text: The must requirement covers the full lifecycle, with four aspects: creation, handover, return and destruction, validity periods, traceability, and handling of loss.
I understand validity periods, like a visitor badge that is valid for one day. But what about traceability?
It means you know who holds every card and every key right now. During a consulting job I asked facilities how many server room keys there were. He said probably three.
And? Did you really find only three?
We found seven! One was still in the drawer of an IT guy who left three years ago, and his successor was using it.
Ha ha, so server room keys can multiply by themselves!
That is why the should item says identification means may only be produced under controlled conditions. Use patented keys that cannot be copied freely, and lock away the card printer and blank cards.
And for high protection needs, what do we add?

You need a strategy to block or invalidate them when lost. Block the card in the system at once, revoke the FIDO key in the identity system. A normal key cannot be disabled remotely, so you may change the lock.
One ISA 2027 change: the time limit requirement for high protection needs was removed. But validity periods are still part of the must requirement, so don't think you can ignore them.

slide.title: ISA 2027 changes
bullets: 4.1.1: time limit for high needs removed
Validity periods still part of must

lines.text: Note this down! Next is 4.1.2, user authentication.
4.1.2 asks: when a user logs in, how do you know it is really them? Two must items: choose the method based on a risk assessment that considers attack scenarios, and follow recognized best practices.

slide.title: 4.1.2 Must
bullets: Consider attacks, e.g. direct internet access

lines.text: What attack scenarios does the text mean?
The example in the text is direct access from the internet. VPN, M365, webmail, remote desktop. Hackers all over the world can try your passwords.
I once audited a company whose VPN was open to the internet with only username and password, and the password policy required just 6 characters. When I asked why, they said it was the vendor default.
That would be hard to explain as a risk assessment.
Right. ISA 2027.1 changed state of the art to recognized best practices, so you can use standards like NIST SP 800-63B as your basis.
Today the mainstream view focuses on password length and blocking leaked passwords, not forcing a change every 90 days, which just ends with Password01, Password02.
Ha ha, I think I know people who set passwords like that.
And what about should, high, and very high protection needs?

slide.title: 4.1.2 Requirements by level
bullets: Should: strong passwords, PAM or 2FA for admins
High: disable when idle, stop brute force

lines.text: Should asks for at least strong passwords, and better methods for privileged accounts, like PAM or two-factor. High protection needs add measures like monitoring unusual logins, automatic logout, and account lockout.
For very high protection needs, strong authentication such as two-factor is required before accessing that data.
So if we turn on MFA for the whole company, are we done?
That is the most common misunderstanding. The auditor will ask: do domain admins have MFA? What about the admin interfaces of firewalls and switches? And the cloud consoles?
Many companies enable MFA for normal staff, but not for IT's own admin accounts, because it is annoying. But those are exactly the accounts hackers want most.
Wow, it is darkest right under the lamp. That is so dangerous!
I recommend a system authentication overview: for each system, is it internet facing, what are the protection needs, which method is used. That table is your risk assessment evidence.
Let's sum up! 4.1.1: manage the lifecycle and loss of identification means. 4.1.2: choose authentication by risk, follow best practices, and admins must always have MFA.
In the next part we talk about accounts and access rights. Leaver accounts and Everyone permissions, watch out!

slide.title: Key points
bullets: Register of identification means, loss process

lines.text: Welcome back! This part covers 4.1.3, accounts and login information, and 4.2.1, access rights. Allan, 4.1.3 has so many must requirements!

slide.title: 4.1.3 Account lifecycle
bullets: Disable leavers at once, review regularly

lines.text: Yes, it has the most must items in Chapter 4. The core idea in three phrases: one person, one account; every account has a lifecycle; passwords follow rules.
Accounts must be unique and personal, so you can trace who did what. Shared accounts are not totally forbidden, but they must be regulated and limited to cases where traceability is not needed.
So when is traceability not needed?
For example a production dashboard PC with a read-only account that just shows output numbers. But if everyone shares an account that can change MES data, that is a problem.
Next, the lifecycle. Accounts must be disabled immediately when people leave. When I was an auditor, this was the check with the highest hit rate, by far.
Are leaver accounts that are not disabled really that common?
Very common. I compare last month's leaver list with AD and often find accounts still active three weeks later, sometimes even with logins.
That is scary. Who is using that account?
So ask IT to compare the list with HR once a month. It takes ten minutes. Even better if the HR system is connected to AD.
What must the login information policy cover?

slide.title: Six points of the login policy
bullets: No disclosure, not even to managers or IT
No writing down, no plain-text storage
Change at once if a leak is suspected
Separate private use, change at first login, quality

lines.text: Six points. No disclosure, not even to your boss. Do not write it down or store it in plain text. Change it if you suspect a leak. No reuse for private use. Change the initial password at first login. And quality rules.
On site I once saw a sticky note next to a screen with the ERP password, and it helpfully said: capital P.
Ha ha, how thoughtful. The hackers must be so touched!
Initial passwords must be delivered securely too. Don't email them to the manager to pass on. Send the account and the password through different channels, and force a change at first login.
Should has ten items. Which ones are most often overlooked?

slide.title: 4.1.3 Often overlooked should items
bullets: Disable provider accounts after the task
No interactive login for service accounts

lines.text: First, default accounts and passwords, like admin admin on switches, printers, PLCs, and IP cameras. Second, supplier remote maintenance accounts that are not disabled after the job is done.

Third, accounts in customer systems, such as an employee's account on an OEM portal. When the person leaves, ask the customer to disable it. Fourth, nobody may use service accounts for interactive login.
Note this down! Next, 4.2.1 access rights. The account is the ticket, and the access rights decide which halls the ticket lets you into.
Well said! The 4.2.1 must requirement asks for a process to request, verify, and approve rights, the least privilege principle, and revoking rights that are no longer needed.
And rights must be reviewed regularly: normal accounts, privileged accounts, technical accounts, and even rights in customer IT systems.
Should mentions authorization roles. What does that mean?

It means managing rights by role. A sales assistant role can view orders in the ERP but cannot change prices. New people get rights by role, and when they change jobs they change roles, so rights don't pile up.
I once saw a senior employee who moved from quality to sales and then to purchasing. He could still open the folders of all three departments and didn't even know it.
Wow, that is the famous privilege creep!
And the auditor's favorite: file server folders shared with Everyone. Before the assessment, scan the permissions with a tool. You will get a shock.
What else is required for high and very high protection needs?

slide.title: 4.2.1 Requirements by level
bullets: Keep privileged users away from content

lines.text: For high protection needs, the responsible information owner approves the rights, for example the project manager. IT does not decide alone.

Very high protection needs add two items: content-level encryption, for example with Purview sensitivity labels, so even IT admins cannot see the content. And shorter review cycles, for example every quarter.
How do we keep access reviews from becoming just paperwork?
The key is that the information owner confirms, instead of IT printing a list and stamping it. Rights that are not needed must really be removed, and the removal is recorded.
Chapter 4 summary! Manage the lifecycle of identification means, choose authentication by risk, one account per person, disable leavers at once, and keep rights minimal and reviewed.
